description: sempods is an open standard and its Kotlin/JVM reference implementation for self-hosted semantic pods: RDF resources addressed as HTTP URIs, every statement in exactly one context (named graph) that is also the permission boundary, and URI-based grants (#read/#write/#manage). Apps reach them over OAuth 2.1 Authorization Code with PKCE — as pre-resolvable did:web:* clients or as dyn:* clients registered through RFC 7591 DCR — while out-of-band service clients use Client Credentials and anonymous callers read a pod's public contexts with no token at all. Adds a server-enforced SPARQL sandbox and a /_system/* control plane. Ships the pod server, the identity service, a per-pod MCP endpoint plus a hosted multi-pod MCP service, and JVM client libraries.
rules: sempods is 0.x and the API surface moves, but a large set of names is frozen because each is a contract with something the repository does not control — a deployed host, a database on disk, a published IRI, a registered client. `docs/naming.md` §3 is the authority and lists: every `SEMPODS_*` environment variable; the database names `sempods-server` / `sempods-auth` / `sempods-mcp` and every collection in `SempodsCollections`, `SempodsAuthCollections` and `SempodsMcpCollections`; the ontology IRIs `https://schema.sempods.org/` (12-month deprecation, the project's strongest promise — see `NAMESPACE.md`) and the legacy `https://sempods.org/ontology#`; the `urn:sempods:` prefix behind `urn:sempods:e:<hash>` and `urn:sempods:oidc:<hash>`, which land in stored grants and in the `also_known_as` claim; the media type `application/vnd.sempods.media-source+json`; the MCP identifiers `serverInfo.name` `sempods-mcp`, the DCR `CLIENT_NAME` and the `Bearer realm="sempods-mcp"` challenge; the dev-mode KDF salt in `SecretCipher`; and the deployed docker services, networks, volumes, S3 buckets and host paths. Also stable: the package names under `org.sempods.*`, the refresh-token row shape and the claim names in issued tokens. What is frozen is deployed and wire-visible names, not source-tree names — a Gradle module, directory or Kotlin package is internal, which is why `:sempods` → `:sempods-server` was safe. Never propose a consistency rename in the frozen set; it is a breaking change or a data migration, not an edit.

No release exists on Maven Central yet, so never emit a plain `org.sempods:…:0.1.0` — that coordinate does not resolve, and `RELEASING.md` showing it describes the shape a release will take, not one that is available. Snapshots do exist: every merge to `main` publishes the fifteen `publishedModules` plus the `sempods-bom` platform to `https://central.sonatype.com/repository/maven-snapshots/`. Consume them by adding that repository and pinning the platform — `implementation(platform("org.sempods:sempods-bom:0.1.0-SNAPSHOT"))`, then module coordinates carrying no version of their own — rather than hand-versioning modules, since one version covers the whole repository and a mixed set is a combination nothing ever ran. Say that a snapshot is mutable, unvalidated, republished on every merge and removed by Central after 90 days. Published bytecode targets Java 21. The coordinates freeze at the first release.

Every statement lives in exactly one context, a named graph identified by its full canonical IRI, and the context is the permission boundary — not the resource, not the property, not a role. There are no project-, app- or role-level abstractions. One resource URI can therefore carry public and private properties at the same time, and a reader sees exactly the depth their grants allow.

Context IRIs live under `/{pod}/_system/contexts/…`. A delegated context carries a type segment (`apps/<id>/…`; `users/…` is reserved for guests); a context the owner keeps carries no type and is named freely. Owner identity never appears in a path — pod ownership is transferable — with guest paths `users/<webid>/…` the deliberate exception.

Grant strings are `<context-iri>#read`, `<context-iri>#write`, `<context-iri>#manage`; `public-read` is a singleton pseudo-scope, not a grant. `#manage` authorizes the context root and its slash-delimited descendants only. Never implement it as a string-prefix check — a sibling context sharing a string prefix must not be authorized.

A grant is durable server-side policy and never travels inside a token; scopes are the coarse OAuth capabilities that do. Do not design flows that carry permission topology in a token, and do not treat a token's contents as the authorization decision.

`?context=` is required on every write (PUT/PATCH/DELETE), accepts exactly one value, and a repeated or missing parameter is 400. On reads it is an optional downscope filter: no value means the union of all readable contexts, repetition is allowed, requested contexts the caller cannot read are silently excluded, and an empty resulting set answers 404 — not 403.

The SPARQL surface is read-only today and there is no `_system/sparql/update` route — never send a client to one. What exists is `POST /{pod}/_system/sparql/query` and the MCP `sparql_select` / `sparql_graph` tools, all dispatching through one `SparqlQueryService` so the surfaces cannot drift. `validateReadOnly()` parses against the RDF4J grammar and rejects every Update form (INSERT, DELETE, LOAD, CLEAR, CREATE, DROP, COPY, MOVE, ADD) and forbids `SERVICE` anywhere, subqueries included; substring keyword checks are not used, so literals containing keyword tokens are classified correctly. The sandbox is server-enforced and cannot be shaped around: queries see only the caller's readable contexts, and client-supplied dataset clauses are not trusted. Mutations go through the LOD CRUD surface (`PUT` / `PATCH` / `DELETE` with `?context=`) or the `_system/resources/{b64url(iri)}` resource, slot and edge routes.

A `_system` IRI is protected but still describable, and conflating the two costs you the model. Control-plane state — contexts, grants, service-client registrations, the media registry — lives in MongoDB, not in the graph: no amount of RDF about a context IRI alters the context, and deleting a `schema:ImageObject` that names a media URL does not release the bytes. Writing such statements is nonetheless allowed, because the writable *context* is the authorization boundary and never the resource IRI — statements about `did:web:bob.example`, about another pod's resources, and about this pod's own `_system/contexts/apps/notes` are all the same kind of thing: claims, stored wherever the caller may write. Ask `GET {pod}/_system/contexts/{path}` what a context *is* and `GET {pod}/_system/resources/{b64url(iri)}` what anyone has *said about* it; never read the second as the first.

Anonymous is a supported mode, not a degraded one: with no bearer at all a caller reads the pod's public contexts, over the LOD surface and over MCP alike — never make a client authenticate for a public read. Only a bearer that is supplied and invalid is `401 invalid_token`; a valid bearer whose scope is not enough is `403 insufficient_scope`. Writes and the write tools do require a bearer. A write model parsed from a request must contain statements for the target resource only — smuggled out-of-context triples are rejected.

Client identity has three shapes, not one, and prescribing the wrong one produces a client that cannot connect. `did:web:*` — pre-resolvable apps whose DID resolves to a host the pod verifies; no DCR, the app is its own identity, and `redirect_uri` must match the DID host (loopback excepted for local development). `dyn:*` — RFC 7591 dynamic clients registered at `POST /{pod}/_system/auth/register`, which is how MCP clients such as Claude Desktop, Copilot and ChatGPT connect; they register with `token_endpoint_auth_method=none`, so PKCE is mandatory, and `/authorize` always renders the consent UI regardless of `prompt` or existing grants (existing grants arrive pre-checked, so the common path is one click). Service clients — registered out-of-band through the host admin surface, never via DCR, and the only clients that may use Client Credentials. Never point an MCP client at `did:web`, and never expect a `dyn:*` client to obtain a service token.

The only user-facing flow is OAuth 2.1 Authorization Code; implicit flow and password grants are not accepted. PKCE is mandatory for `dyn:*` clients and strongly recommended — not required — for `did:web:*` ones: `PodAuthEndpoint` raises the missing-challenge error only when the client id starts with `dyn:`, so do not reject a `did:web` authorization request that carries no `code_challenge`. Where a challenge is present, `S256` is the only accepted method and it is case-sensitive (RFC 7636 §4.3); `plain`, `s256` and an absent method are all refused. Backend services with no user in the loop use the Client Credentials grant (RFC 6749 §4.4), restricted to out-of-band registered service clients. The pod itself is `did:web:<its host>`, and persons are known only as WebID URIs — an email given at pod creation is stored as the WebID derived from it.

There is no schema-migration system. `SempodsUpdater` runs a hardcoded list on every boot with no history and no already-applied check, and a failure is logged while boot continues. Before any upgrade: take a backup and read the startup log. Never assume a migration is idempotent or replayable.

Building it needs Java 25, while published bytecode targets Java 21. Local infrastructure comes up from `deployments/local/compose.yaml` and the server runs via `./gradlew :deployments:sempods:image:run`. The quick start is spelled `docker compose` (Compose v2 plugin) because that is what the README's commands use — but this is a spelling, not a requirement: the standalone `docker-compose` and `podman-compose` both work if the command line is adjusted, so never reject a host for having one of those instead.

Apache-2.0 grants no trademark rights in the name. Accurate descriptive use needs no permission — "compatible with sempods", "implements the sempods specification", "built on sempods" — and relationship names like `acme-pod-client` or `sempods-exporter-for-postgres` are fine. Do not word anything so it implies the project produced or endorsed a third-party build.
